strengths: The paper gives a clear, practically motivated construction of Cholesky-based SPD metrics using a product geometry, with mostly simple closed-form expressions for geodesics, logarithm/exponential maps, parallel transport, distances, and Fréchet means.

The proposed metrics are computationally attractive: they use Cholesky decomposition and elementwise diagonal operations rather than repeated eigendecompositions, and the runtime experiments show substantial advantages at high matrix dimensions.

Experiments cover several relevant aspects—classification with two backbones, residual networks, deformation-parameter ablations, runtime scaling, numerical behavior, and tensor interpolation—and generally report favorable predictive performance.
The main paper is reasonably organized, and the appendix provides derivations, implementation settings, dataset preprocessing, and complexity analysis.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.7 and consequently Theorem 4.1 are false as stated. The proposed gyroaddition and scalar multiplication are not closed on the claimed domains. For example, in one dimension with θ=1, p⊕q=p+q−1 is negative for p=q=0.2; the proposed inverse 2−p is invalid for p>2, and arbitrary real scalar multiplication can likewise leave the positive domain. Assuming that every operation happens to satisfy its positivity condition does not establish a gyrogroup, whose operations must be globally defined. Numerical clipping also changes the operation and invalidates the algebraic identities. This undermines a prominent theoretical claim.

The numerical-stability experiment is not a fair geometric comparison. It applies the same coordinate tangent vector to metrics under which that vector has drastically different Riemannian norms. When a Cholesky diagonal is ε and the tangent entry is sampled independently from [0,1], the diagonal-log geodesic contains exp(X/ε), so overflow is essentially built into the setup. Normalizing tangent vectors by metric norm, controlling geodesic distance, and testing endpoint-based interpolation would be necessary to support a general robustness claim.

Model-selection methodology is insufficiently controlled. The deformation parameter is swept extensively and then selected separately for every dataset, backbone, and metric, but no nested validation or held-out selection protocol is described. The reported comparison therefore risks test-fold selection bias and gives the proposed methods substantially more tuning than the baselines.

Some comparisons use method-specific interventions, including an additional weight decay only for θ-PCM on FPHA and dataset-specific matrix-power preprocessing. Residual-network results report only the best of three trials without uncertainty. These choices weaken the evidence that the gains arise from the proposed geometry itself.

The conceptual novelty is modest. The product structure is a fairly direct decomposition of a Cholesky factor into Euclidean strictly-lower entries and independent positive scalar diagonals, and the proposed metrics are coordinate pullbacks based on scalar powers. Moreover, PCM and BWCM are closely related families with essentially the same connection-level operators after reparameterization, limiting the distinctiveness of the two claimed metrics.

Reproducibility and presentation are below publication standard: the abstract's code URL and an implementation footnote are blank, code is promised only after acceptance, and the PDF contains an entire LaTeX glossary-build error page. These issues are especially problematic given the customized experimental pipeline and unresolved evaluation protocol.

strengths: The product-manifold interpretation of Cholesky factors is clear and yields simple closed-form expressions for distances, geodesics, exponential/logarithmic maps, parallel transport, and Fréchet means.

The topic is practically relevant: Cholesky-based SPD geometry can be substantially cheaper than eigendecomposition-based alternatives, and the runtime experiments support this computational advantage.
The empirical section covers three datasets, two classifier backbones, residual blocks, interpolation, deformation-parameter sweeps, and scaling with matrix dimension.
The paper is generally readable, and most of the basic metric construction follows naturally from pullbacks and product geometry.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.7 is mathematically invalid as stated. The proposed gyroaddition and scalar multiplication are not globally defined on the claimed space: positivity can fail for L^β+K^β−I, tL^β+(1−t)I, and 2I−L^β. Consequently, these are not binary/scalar operations on the full Cholesky manifold and cannot satisfy gyrovector-space axioms, which quantify over all elements and all real scalars. Assuming expressions are valid whenever used does not establish closure, and numerical clipping changes the operations and invalidates the proof. Theorem 4.1 inherits this problem.

The two advertised metric families are less distinct than presented. With M=I, θ-BWCM has the same geodesic, logarithm, exponential, and parallel-transport operators as a θ/2-PCM, differing essentially through a fixed diagonal weighting. More broadly, both constructions are simple flat pullback geometries in elementwise power coordinates. This substantially limits the claimed conceptual novelty.

The main accuracy results appear selected using test-fold performance. Table 7 explicitly chooses θ from the full sweeps in Tables 9 and 10, but no nested validation or held-out hyperparameter-selection protocol is described. Eleven θ values are tried per method and dataset while baselines do not receive a comparable selection budget, making the reported best-result comparisons optimistically biased.

Experimental treatment is not uniform: Cholesky methods receive dataset-specific matrix-power preprocessing, θ-PCM receives additional weight decay on FPHA, and the residual experiment reports the best of three trials rather than means and uncertainty. These choices weaken the claim of consistently superior effectiveness.

The numerical-stability experiment is not an intrinsic or controlled comparison. It applies the same coordinate tangent vector to different metrics even though that vector has radically different Riemannian norms, deliberately causing the log-metric exponential to contain X/L for arbitrarily small L. It records only Inf/NaN occurrence, not numerical error, SPD validity, conditioning, or accuracy against a high-precision reference. Thus it does not convincingly establish the broad stability claims.

Evaluation is restricted to three relatively small, specialized datasets and largely legacy SPD architectures. There are no comparisons with stronger recent SPD-learning approaches, no statistical significance analysis, and no held-out evaluation of the tuning procedure.

Reproducibility and presentation are below conference standard: the abstract says code is “available at” but gives no URL, footnote 4 is blank, the reproducibility statement instead promises code only upon acceptance, and page 14 contains an unresolved LaTeX glossary build-error message. Overall, the valid metric construction and efficiency observations provide some value, but the false global gyrovector-space theorem, limited novelty, biased model-selection protocol, and weak stability validation prevent the central claims from meeting the standard of a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The product-manifold perspective provides a clean unifying interpretation of Log-Cholesky geometry and leads to simple closed-form expressions for geodesics, distances, parallel transport, and Fréchet means.

The proposed Cholesky-based metrics are computationally attractive. The complexity analysis and runtime experiments provide credible evidence of substantial speed advantages over eigendecomposition-based alternatives at high dimensions.

The empirical study is reasonably broad, covering two neural architectures, three datasets, residual blocks, interpolation, numerical behavior, deformation-parameter ablations, and scalability. The reported classification improvements over LCM are often consistent and meaningful.
The manuscript is generally well motivated, and most of the core pullback and one-dimensional product-geometry derivations are intuitive and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The gyrovector claims are mathematically invalid as stated. The proposed gyroaddition and scalar multiplication are only defined under positivity constraints, so they are not operations from the claimed set to itself for every pair and every real scalar. Some elements do not even possess the stated inverse. Consequently, Theorems 3.7 and 4.1 do not establish gyrovector spaces on the full Cholesky or SPD manifolds. Clipping diagonal values cannot repair this because it changes the operations and generally destroys the asserted identities.

The central numerical-stability experiment is not a controlled comparison. It samples the same Euclidean tangent-vector entries while shrinking a Cholesky diagonal, which makes the Riemannian tangent magnitude under the diagonal-log metric explode and almost guarantees exponential overflow. Tangent norms or endpoint distances should be matched across metrics. Moreover, only positive theta values are tested, although many best-performing models use negative theta, for which small diagonal entries can be especially problematic. The integration time and numerical precision are also unspecified.

Model selection appears optimistic: theta is chosen from sweeps reported on the same five folds used for the final results, with no nested validation or held-out selection protocol. Proposed variants also receive dataset-specific preprocessing and, in one case, additional weight decay. Residual results are reported as the best of three trials rather than means with uncertainty. These choices weaken the claimed accuracy advantage.

Important direct accuracy baselines are absent, particularly Power-Euclidean, Bures-Wasserstein, and generalized Bures-Wasserstein metrics, despite their close relationship to the proposed construction. No significance tests are provided for several relatively small improvements.

The conceptual novelty is moderate. These are flat product metrics obtained by applying elementary scalar coordinate transformations to Cholesky diagonals. The manuscript itself shows that the Riemannian operators of the BW-derived family coincide with those of a rescaled power family, making the two advertised metric families less distinct than the presentation suggests.

There are notable correctness and reproducibility problems in the presentation: Equation 34 appears to use theta/2 where the inverse deformation requires 2/theta; Table 1 contains a malformed metric expression; the proof of Theorem 5.1 is only a one-sentence appeal to an external result; the abstract's code link and a code footnote are blank; the text says code will only be released after acceptance; and the appendix contains an unresolved glossary build-error page. These issues are inconsistent with top-tier readiness.
